name: idempotent-client
intent: Give every logical write a stable identity - a client-minted idempotency key or a naturally idempotent operation form - and reuse it on every attempt, so a retry sent after an unknown outcome is recognised as the same operation and cannot apply the change twice.
problem: A write that crosses a network boundary has three outcomes for the caller: committed, not committed, or unknown - a timeout or dropped connection after the server may already have committed. Because retry middleware, SDK auto-retry, at-least-once brokers and human resubmission all replay the call, the unknown case turns into a duplicate effect (a second charge, order, notification or increment) unless the receiver can recognise the replay as the same logical operation.
context: Write paths over a network or a redelivering broker where the caller or its transport owns the retries and the effect is not idempotent on its own: endpoints that create or mutate (POST, PATCH, delta updates), message handlers under at-least-once delivery, job runners replaying after a crash, and offline clients resubmitting queued edits. It matters most when the effect escapes the database - payments, e-mails, webhooks, inventory holds - or when the operation's cost or audit trail makes a duplicate unacceptable.
benefits: Duplicate attempts collapse to one logical effect: create, charge, increment and notify happen once even when the request is replayed.
Retries become safe by default, so middleware, SDK auto-retry and user resubmission need no per-call exception list.
Unknown-outcome failures become resolvable: replaying with the same key returns the recorded outcome instead of guessing whether the first attempt landed.
Side effects outside the transaction (payments, e-mails, webhooks, reservations) stop being a source of double execution that no rollback can undo.
The key doubles as a stable correlation id for logs, audit and cross-service propagation, and makes duplicate rates measurable.
At-least-once delivery becomes usable end to end - effectively-once processing - without distributed transactions.
tradeoffs: The receiver needs a durable key -> outcome record with an index and a retention policy at least as long as a retry can arrive; that store is new infrastructure to operate and pay for.

Correctness depends on writing the key and the business effect in one atomic step; a naive check-then-write leaves a crash window in which the effect is applied but the key is not recorded (or the reverse).

Key generation becomes a correctness dependency: minting the key inside the retry loop, deriving it from the payload, or holding it only in memory disables the guarantee while the code still looks protected.
Concurrent duplicates must be arbitrated by the store (unique constraint, conditional upsert, lock), which serialises them on one key and can create hot rows or contention.
Naturally idempotent forms change the API contract: absolute writes and conditional updates reject edits that a blind retry used to clobber, so callers must handle the conflict.
Retained key/outcome data is a privacy and storage liability - keys can leak payload information, and an unbounded retention window grows without limit.

Idempotency is not freshness: replaying an absolute value can still overwrite newer state unless the write is guarded by a version or ETag, and the guarantee does not extend downstream unless the key is propagated.

participants.responsibility: Owns the identity of the logical operation: mints the key before the first attempt, reuses it verbatim on every retry, persists it across process restarts, and restricts automatic retries to operations it may replay.
The stable name of one logical operation - a random UUID or request id with enough entropy to be unique, never derived from retry-varying state and never reused for different work.

The parameters the key is bound to; the receiver compares them (or a hash) on a replay, so a reused key with different content is reported as misuse instead of silently returning an unrelated outcome.
Decides which failures are worth replaying, with what backoff and what attempt bound, and only replays operations that are declared idempotent or carry a key.
Accepts the key, records key -> outcome atomically with the business effect, replays the recorded outcome for a duplicate, and answers 'already applied' as success rather than as an error.
The durable inbox/keyset holding the key, a request fingerprint, the outcome or an in-progress marker, and an expiry; its uniqueness constraint arbitrates two simultaneous duplicates.
Keeps the result (status and body, or an in-progress marker for work that cannot join the transaction) so that a replay returns the original answer instead of re-executing.

use_cases: Payments and refunds: a charge call times out, the client replays it with the same idempotency key, the account is debited once and the original response is returned.
Order or booking creation over a flaky mobile link: the app mints the operation id, stores it with the queued submission and resubmits until it sees the recorded outcome.
Queue consumers under at-least-once delivery: a handler that applied the command but crashed before acknowledging deduplicates on the command id after redelivery.
Offline-first field clients: queued edits are replayed after reconnect, each carrying an operation id and a version guard, so replays neither double-apply nor clobber newer data.
Batch and cron jobs: a failed step re-runs from the last checkpoint and replays keyed operations instead of repeating increments or re-sending notifications.

Webhook and double-submitted forms: the same logical submission forwarded twice by a browser retry or a gateway is applied once, and the id is propagated to downstream services so each tier deduplicates its own work.

Notification and messaging systems: a notification service that resends an e-mail or push notification after a timeout deduplicates by a message-level idempotency ID; the handler is idempotent (no-op if already delivered).

Pub/Sub message handling: Google Cloud Pub/Sub and Amazon SQS provide at-least-once delivery by default; Cloud Run handlers or SQS consumers must deduplicate by message ID or an embedded idempotency key to achieve effectively-once semantics.

Cross-service state propagation: a hotel-booking service emits a 'booking confirmed' event to a loyalty-point service; the loyalty service deduplicates by the booking event ID and only credits points once.

Saga pattern compensation: in a distributed hotel+flight booking saga, the compensate-flight step is idempotent – it checks whether the flight was already cancelled before cancelling; the saga retry with the same step ID does not double-cancel.
Financial reconciliation: a nightly reconciliation job detects duplicate charge entries by idempotency key and flags them for refund rather than assuming every logged charge is a valid one.

API gateway rate limiting with idempotency: a gateway that rate-limits by (client-id, idempotency-key) treats retries of the same logical operation as a single request, preventing retry storms from exhausting rate-limit buckets.

Kafka's idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true, the default since Kafka 3.0): the producer obtains a Producer ID for its session and stamps every batch with a per-(partition, Producer ID) sequence number, so the broker - not application code - discards batches that were already appended when the client retries, giving exactly-once writes into the log without an application-level key. The guarantee holds only within one producer session; a transactional.id is needed to recover idempotence across restarts.

AWS EC2 RunInstances ClientToken: the caller supplies a unique case-sensitive token (up to 64 ASCII characters) and a retried launch returns the original result instead of starting a second instance; if the caller omits the token EC2 generates one, so the protection is on by default. Tokens are scope-bound - zonal idempotency when an Availability Zone or SubnetId is given, otherwise regional - so a retry that changes zone or parameters fails with IdempotentParameterMismatch instead of deduplicating.

MDN / IETF Idempotency-Key header: the emerging standard for client-minted keys on POST and PATCH - a replay returns the first recorded result, a key still being processed answers 409, and a key replayed with a different payload fingerprint answers 422 Unprocessable Content, so the client can distinguish 'already done' from 'still in flight' from 'key misused'.
avoid_when: The operation is already naturally idempotent - a PUT that sets absolute state, a DELETE, or an update guarded by a version/ETag: use plain optimistic concurrency (Version Number) and skip the key store.
A duplicate is genuinely harmless (pure reads, recomputable projections, counters that tolerate a double count): the store costs more than the anomaly it prevents.
At-most-once is the honest requirement (an irreversible external action the business prefers to miss rather than repeat): fail visibly and reconcile by hand instead.

The transport already covers it: a broker with duplicate detection, a transactional consumer checkpoint, or an exactly-once stream processor may make an application key unnecessary - though none of them covers effects outside that transaction.
The server contract cannot be changed (a third-party API without key support): use client-side single-flight plus an explicit reconciliation query instead of pretending the retry is safe.
anti_patterns: Minting the key inside the retry loop: every attempt becomes a new logical operation and the pattern silently does nothing.
Deriving the key from the payload or the attempt number: corrected parameters produce a new key (so the retry duplicates) while two identical legitimate submissions collide on one key.
Check-then-insert without a unique constraint or an atomic conditional write, so two concurrent duplicates both pass the check.
Expiring deduplication records faster than a retry can arrive - including manual replays from a dead-letter queue - which reopens the duplicate window.
Retrying every failure, including validation errors and business rejections, and storing the rejection as 'the outcome', so permanently failing calls look like successful replays.
Recording an in-progress marker and never reconciling it, leaving operations that can neither be safely replayed nor completed after a crash between the external call and the completion update.
Reusing one key for a batch or for unrelated operations, which makes the store collapse distinct work into a single recorded outcome.
design_principles: Design for the unknown: because 'no response' does not mean 'no effect', every replayable write needs an identity the receiver can recognise.
Single responsibility: the caller owns the operation identity, the receiver owns detection and the recorded outcome, and neither infers it from the other.
Atomicity as a boundary: the deduplication marker and the business effect commit together or not at all.
Idempotency by construction: prefer naturally idempotent forms (absolute upserts, conditional writes) over bookkeeping, and keep keys for operations that cannot be expressed that way.
End-to-end propagation: a guarantee that stops at the first hop is not a guarantee - pass the operation id down the call chain.
Explicitness over magic: declare which operations are retryable instead of letting middleware infer it from HTTP verbs or naming conventions.
best_practices: Mint the key once per logical operation, before the first attempt, from a cryptographically secure random source (UUIDv4), and persist it with the pending work so a restart resumes the same operation.

Bind the key to the request content – store a fingerprint (SHA-256 of the business-meaningful fields plus method and path, excluding volatile headers and timestamps) alongside the key and compare it on replay; per the IETF idempotency-key draft, a replay whose fingerprint differs is key misuse (422 Unprocessable Content) and a replay while the first attempt is still in flight is a conflict (409 with Retry-After) - neither should silently return the recorded outcome.
Commit the marker and the effect in the same transaction, and let a uniqueness constraint arbitrate concurrent duplicates instead of a read-check in application code.
Return the original recorded outcome for duplicates (or the current state with a documented note), and answer 'already applied' as success.

Retry only replay-safe calls: RFC 9110 idempotent methods, or operations explicitly declared idempotent; disable blanket auto-retry for unsafe methods and rely on the key when a POST must be replayed.
Propagate the key to downstream calls made while processing, and log detected duplicates as a metric so a rising duplicate rate is visible.

Size the deduplication window to the worst-case replay horizon: broker redelivery delay + dead-letter queue TTL + manual resubmission latency; expire keys deliberately rather than never, but never before that horizon.

Distinguish permanent failures (400, 401, 403, 404, 409, 422) – which must never be retried with the same key – from transient failures (408, 429, 500, 502, 503, 504) – which should be retried with back-off.
For batch or multi-item operations, assign one key per logical item so that one item's failure retries without re-executing unrelated items in the same logical batch.

Keep the idempotency store transactionally coupled to the business data: write the key record and the business effect in the same DB transaction so a crash cannot apply the effect without recording the key.

Instrument duplicate detection as a metric (e.g. `idempotency.duplicates_detected` counter) and alert when the duplicate rate exceeds a threshold – it signals upstream retry storms or broker misconfiguration.

For global or high-stakes financial operations, use a strongly consistent store (e.g. Cloud Spanner) rather than an eventually consistent one; a stale read of the key set can let a duplicate execute before the prior write is visible.
sources: Hohpe, G. & Woolf, B., Enterprise Integration Patterns (2003) – Idempotent Receiver: duplicates are inevitable in messaging, and idempotency is achieved either by explicit de-duping or by defining message semantics to be idempotent.

Amazon Web Services, 'Amazon SQS FIFO Queues – Deduplication and Exactly-Once Processing' (2023): content-based deduplication via SHA-256 hash of message body, or explicit deduplication ID; guarantees each message is delivered exactly once and processed exactly once.

Oskar Dudycz, 'Outbox, Inbox Patterns and Delivery Guarantees Explained' (Event-Driven.io, Dec 2020): at-least-once delivery requires either the Outbox pattern (producer side) or Inbox pattern (consumer side); both use a transactional table as the durable log and enable idempotent processing by recording processed message IDs.

Google Cloud, 'What is Idempotency? A Guide to API Reliability' (Cloud Google Discover, 2024): covers Cloud Run + Pub/Sub at-least-once delivery requiring idempotent handlers, Memorystore (Redis) for short-term key caching, Cloud Spanner for globally consistent high-stakes financial idempotency keys.

ByteByteGo, 'Mastering Idempotency: Building Reliable APIs' (Feb 2025): elevator-button analogy; payment processing double-charge prevention; idempotent vs non-idempotent HTTP methods; implementation walkthrough with idempotency key header.

Zuplo, 'Implementing Idempotency Keys in REST APIs – A Complete Guide' (Aug 2025): parameter-drift detection, conflict resolution (409 vs cached response), key lifecycle management, and integration with API gateways and client SDKs.
PayPal API Reference, 'Idempotency' (PayPal Developer Docs): use of PayPal-Request-Id header for POST requests; covers retry behavior, outcome caching, and the 24-hour idempotency window.

MDN Web Docs, 'Idempotency-Key header': client-side contract for POST/PATCH - unique key per logical request, same key on retry; 400 when a required key is missing, 409 while the first attempt is still processing, 422 when fingerprinting detects a different payload.

IETF, 'The Idempotency-Key HTTP Request Header' (draft-ietf-httpapi-idempotency-key-header-07): normative retry semantics - replay returns the previously completed result (success or error), 409 for an in-flight key, 422 for key reuse with a different payload, key fingerprint derived from the request, and server-managed key expiry.

Apache Kafka, 'Producer Configs': enable.idempotence (default true since 3.0) gives exactly-once semantics per partition within a producer session; requires acks=all, retries > 0 and max.in.flight.requests.per.connection <= 5, and conflicts throw ConfigException; transactional.id extends idempotence across sessions.

Amazon Web Services, 'Ensuring idempotency in Amazon EC2 API requests': ClientToken (unique, case-sensitive, up to 64 ASCII characters, auto-generated if omitted) and the distinction between zonal idempotency (explicit Availability Zone or SubnetId) and regional idempotency, including IdempotentParameterMismatch when a token is replayed with different parameters.

InfoWorld, 'Why an idempotency key isn't an idempotency guarantee': the four-assumptions test (claim, intent, memory, boundary) - a key yields exactly-once effects, not exactly-once delivery, and fails when the claim races, the fingerprint ignores meaningful fields, the cached outcome is unsafe to replay, or an external provider sits outside the key's boundary.
